cells.tense: You are reading the moment right now, with nothing in the way.
cells.ask: Name tonight, out loud or on paper, the one thing you see clearly about how someone close to you is doing — and leave it unverified.
cells.core:
You can look at something half-formed and see what it actually needs. Not by reasoning your way there — you just know, and it has a habit of turning out right. People bring you things before they're ready to be shared, because you don't rush what's unfolding. And you're easy about not knowing. You can sit with a question open for a while and nothing in you panics.

That steadiness comes from giving your attention where something is actually moving, so less of it goes to what won't grow. What this asks of you is to let your read stay partial. Say what you see, then wait and let the thing keep unfolding past what you saw.
cells.sheetLine: You see what's growing and you can wait for it.
cells.verb: Knowing what to attend to before the reasons arrive
cells.place: Where what is growing gets tended

cells.tense: You're already living past this moment, and it hasn't happened yet.
cells.ask: Take one thing you're tending and write down the single next step, then leave the rest blank for a week.
cells.core:
There's a picture ahead of how this turns out, and you're gathering everything that might be needed for it. More reading, more checking, more angles — each one feels like preparing. Meanwhile the thing in front of you hasn't been touched since you started getting ready. What you see directly is real. It's just being asked to cover more than this moment contains.

When you stockpile against a future that hasn't arrived, that work starts crowding out the work. Preparing stands in for what you meant to do. So pick one thing you're bringing along and put it down — not forever, just past the point where you've handled the next step. What's left unfinished stays unfinished, and that's allowed.

cells.tense: You knew something once, and you've been standing at that door ever since.
cells.ask: Answer one small question — what to make for dinner — using only your own preference, no second opinion.
cells.core:
Every read you have about what's growing near you comes with a question mark attached now. What you notice about the people and work around you arrives, then gets checked against someone else's version, and the checking is where it ends. So you wait to be told what you already sensed. What got lost isn't that you see — you still see. It's that the read you get feels like it needs a witness before you'll move on it.

Start with something small, where the stakes are nothing, and act as though your own read is the one that counts. It will feel thin at first. Go by it anyway, and see where it takes you.

cells.tense: Decisions you call random keep landing, and you're not the one credited with making them.
cells.ask: Pick one choice you've been calling a coin flip, say who made it, and own what happens next.
cells.core:
You keep finding yourself in the right place at the right time and calling it luck. A decision gets made, it works out, and later you can't say how you arrived there. Meanwhile the way you handle what's growing is more careful than you give yourself credit for — it shows in what you keep alive and what you quietly let go.

When you're in step with this, the steps are there if someone asks. You can say why you chose it, and the reasons come without reaching. So the next time something you don't remember choosing goes well, don't hand it to fate. Say it was yours, and watch whether it still holds up.

attempts.check: The draft wants to say the person's flashes of knowing arrive whole and untaught, but the record only supports accuracy and surprise, not a prior room where saying it went badly, so that stays out of Too Little. A reader could reasonably say they do argue with their own perceptions and doubt them for weeks rather than landing without argument, so each cell narrows to the moment of knowing rather than the whole life. The asks survive a wrong read because each is something done in the next day about a plain decision, needing no money or other person, and still teaches them something. The sentence that serves me more than them is 'you already know,' which flatters the reader instead of handing over the moment they can test, so it is dropped.

It also borrowed 'capacity' from the record's own vocabulary and 'the claim on it' from the house's line, neither of which belongs on glass. A reader could reasonably say they do second-guess themselves and sleep on big choices before moving, so each cell stays at the moment a decision gets made rather than the shape of a whole life. All four asks survive a wrong read because each is one small act about a plain choice, needing no money, no other person and no free afternoon, and each still teaches something even if my read misses. The sentence that serves me more than them is 'you already know,' which flatters instead of handing over something testable, so it is gone.
